sections.h: Four steps from goal to action

### Name

### Decide
Record the important choice and its reason. The decision stays linked to the choice and the reason behind it.
### Deliver
Place actions, owners, and what must happen first under the decision. The next step has a clear place in the thread. A blocked path becomes a question the team can act on.
### Revisit
Use new information to review the choice while keeping the original reason available. The team updates a decision without losing its history.
1. The team starts with an objective and the outcome it wants to change.
2. It records a decision card with the choice and its reason.
3. The decision connects to actions, owners, and what must happen first.
4. The team follows the thread to see what must move, wait, or be resolved.
5. New information goes back to the record. The team can update the decision and keep the earlier reason.

Decision cards hold the choice and its reason. Connected threads show how the decision relates to the objective and the work below it. The team sees what must happen first, what is waiting, and what needs a decision. The Name / Decide / Deliver / Revisit sequence keeps the path easy to follow.

1. Read: See a change in demand or product freshness.
2. Compare: Check the change against current stock and other known issues.
3. Decide: An accountable person selects a practical next action.
4. Review: Keep the decision available for a later check.
Each stock issue has a clear owner and review time. Teams share the same details when they discuss the next action.
With the workflow, staff can:
- see a change in demand or product freshness;
- compare current stock and known problems in one view;
- record the change and choose a next step;
- record the reason for an action;
- discuss the next action with the same details;
- keep the person accountable for the choice; and
- check the decision later and see what happened.

wellbridge-clear-path.title: Make the next service step clear

sections.h: One path from the first question to help
p: People often reach a service before they reach the person responsible for helping them. Repeated forms, unclear questions, and missing details slow the route.
Wellbridge Clear Path has four steps: Start, Share details, Get help, and Continue.
- Start explains what the service is for, what to expect, and what details to share.
- Share details collects basic information and puts it in a simple progress record.
- Get help sends important questions to the right staff member.
- Continue shows what happens after staff take over and what the next service step is.
Each step explains why the service asks for a detail and what happens next. The prompts work together as one guide.
1. The person reads what the service does, what will happen, and what details to share.
2. Simple questions collect the details and show progress.
3. A short record brings the details together for staff.
4. Important questions go to the right staff member.
5. A status view shows the next step.
Questions that need a decision go to the right staff member.
OARC built three connected parts:
- Plain-language prompts that explain why information is requested.
- A readable progress record that prepares relevant administrative details.
- A status view that shows what happens after staff take over.
The questions fill the progress record. Staff get the details they need. The status view shows what happens next.

sections.h: A clearer role for people and teams

Start explains the service. Share details collects information. Get help sends questions to staff. Continue shows what happens next.

vertex-after-launch.title: Give players a reason to return after launch

sections.h: Four steps from play to return
p: The system connects four parts:
1. Play: A player starts with a clear challenge or game moment.
2. Share: A prompt helps the player share something useful from that moment.
3. Recognise: The community makes the shared story visible.
4. Return: The next invitation points the player to another challenge or community moment.

Each part hands work to the next. The challenge creates the starting moment. The prompt carries it beyond the match. Recognition shows that the shared story matters. The next invitation gives players a clear reason to take part again.
OARC built four connected parts:
- a player challenge with a clear task;
- a shared story prompt that helps players share a useful game moment;
- a recognition ritual that makes player effort visible;
- a next invitation that points to the next community moment.

Together, these parts give teams one sequence for planning post-launch participation. Teams set the next challenge, define the useful shared story, show what recognition looks like, and connect that recognition to the next event or challenge.
Product and community teams use the sequence to plan repeatable participation after launch. They:
- set the next challenge instead of relying on more announcements;
- turn a game moment into a useful community shared story;
- show which player efforts deserve recognition;
- connect recognition to the next event or challenge;
- plan from the same play, share, recognise, and return sequence.
The system gives teams a direct path from launch attention to a steady participation rhythm.

botanic-muse-field-notes.title: Turn customer routines into useful stories

sections.h: A clear record for every shared story
p: A contributor shares a routine, image, question, condition, or small observation. The invitation explains participation and intended use before the shared story is sent.

The system stores the shared story, its details, credit details, and permission in one field-note record. Editors review the complete record, then shape the note into a clear story without replacing the contributor’s voice with brand language.
01 — Invite
The team asks for useful detail about a routine or experience. The invitation makes participation and intended use clear.
02 — Capture
The team records the contributor’s words, images, situation, credit, and permission in one field-note record.
03 — Review
An editor checks the complete record before using it. The story stays connected to the contributor’s details and the permission attached to it.
04 — Organise
The team groups notes by theme, question, routine, or editorial need. Editors can find a story that fits a planned piece.
05 — Edit and share
Editors give each note a clear shape while keeping its specific detail. They connect the finished story to a relevant question, routine, or social-story idea.

sections.h: What the team can do with it
p: The archive gives the team one place to collect, review, credit, sort, and publish customer-led beauty stories. Editors work from real detail instead of reducing every shared story to a rating or general endorsement.
The same records support planning. The team can find stories for a theme, prepare new beauty stories, and turn customer routines into social-story ideas.
